p: Three facts change the plan. Please read these before the session.

li.p: GitHub Team plan cannot add required reviewers to environments in a private repo. The org is on the Team plan and the repo is private. GitHub's docs say required reviewers and wait timers are "only available for public repositories" on Free, Pro and Team. So step 0.3 cannot be done as written. Step 0.5 should not happen while we are on Team. The trstringer/manual-approval step is the only approval gate today, and it needs 2 approvals. An environment rule (if we ever get it) needs only 1. Keep the step.

BRAVO_GCP_SA_KEY is an organization secret, shared by many repos. It is not only a mobile secret. A code search finds it in workflows of 51 repos in bfi-finance (backend services, LORA services, web apps). In this repo it is the key that uploads the app to Google Play. Rotating it touches every one of those repos at once.

Why. "Reveal Secret" was built to print this key. The one run failed before it started, so the key was most likely not printed. But anyone who could dispatch the workflow could have read it. Rotation is the safe default.

li.p: What it does: CI uses it with shimataro/ssh-key-action to pull private git dependencies: bfi-flutter-packages (5 references), bfi-flutter-device-integrity, bravo-image-validation-mobile-sdk, bfi-protobuf.
Where it is stored: 5 separate environment secrets, not one repo secret.
Used by 6 workflows: pr-pipeline, on-merge-master, build-sit-uat, build-prod, build-prod-test, build-prod-artifact.

Whose key is it? Not known. bravo-image-validation-mobile-sdk has no deploy keys. One deploy key cannot be attached to several repos. So the key is most likely a personal or machine-user SSH key (inferred, not confirmed). If it is a personal key, it can do anything that person can do on GitHub, including write access.
KNOWN_HOSTS is not a secret value in itself (it holds GitHub's public host keys). It does not need rotation, but check it matches GitHub's current published keys.
Find the account that holds the public key (Q2). An org admin can check the SSH keys of a machine user. Or ask the person who set it up in May 2024.
Create a new key pair. Preferred target: a read-only deploy key per dependency repo (4 keys), or one machine user with read-only access to only those 4 repos. Do not use a personal account.
Update SSH_PRIVATE_KEY in all 5 environments on the same day.
Run one SIT build and one PR pipeline to prove dependencies still resolve.
Delete the old public key from the account that holds it.
All 5 environment secrets show today's date.
The old public key is gone from GitHub (confirmed by the key owner or an org admin).
A PR pipeline run and a build-sit-uat run pass after the change.
The ticket records which account or deploy keys now hold the new key.

Risks and rollback. If the new key is wrong, every build fails at "flutter pub get" for git dependencies. Rollback: keep the old key active until step 4 passes, then delete it. Do the change outside the Monday release-branch cut.

li.p: Q2: Whose account holds the current key? Personal, machine user, or deploy key?
Q5: Move to per-repo deploy keys now, or keep one machine user? Deploy keys mean 4 secrets to manage, but no account can reach other repos.

td.p: A. Rotate in place: new key pair on the same account, update the 5 environment secrets, delete the old public key
Keeps an account we cannot name, which may be personal and may have write access
B. Read-only deploy key per dependency repo (4 keys)
Each key reads one repo only. No person's account involved
4 long-lived keys to rotate. CI needs per-repo key mapping (one SSH key per host alias)

C. GitHub App token: a small internal GitHub App on the 4 repos with Contents read-only. CI gets a token with actions/create-github-app-token (repositories: the 4 repos, permission-contents: read). Git rewrites git@github.com: URLs to HTTPS with the token
No long-lived SSH key. The token lives 1 hour and is revoked at the end of the job. Read-only and limited to 4 repos. GitHub recommends short-lived, well-scoped tokens
Needs an org owner to create the App. The App private key is still a secret, but it can only make read tokens for those 4 repos. Touches 6 workflows

p: Recommended: A this week, then C. Rotation is the urgent part, because the key was exposed to anyone who could dispatch the workflow. C removes the long-lived key. Make C a separate ticket in this epic. If time is short, move it to early Phase 1.

Why. "Reveal Secret" was built to print it too. In this repo it is the service-account key that uploads the prod app to Google Play (r0adkll/upload-google-play, package id.co.bfi.customer, track internal), in build-prod.yml and build-prod-test.yml.

li.p: It is an organization secret, last updated 9 Apr 2026. It is not stored in this repo or in its environments.

A GitHub code search for secrets.BRAVO_GCP_SA_KEY finds 51 repos in bfi-finance. Examples: bravo-user-iam-service, bravo-agency-service, bravo-calculation-service, bfi-operation-api, lora-cdc-bridge-service, lora-ndf-4w. The search count can include old or archived repos.
Because it is one org secret, updating it updates every repo at once. That makes the swap easy, and a bad key breaks all of them at once.
The same key both deploys backend services to GCP (inferred from the other repos) and publishes the customer app to Google Play. One leaked key can do both.

BFI already uses keyless Google sign-in (Workload Identity Federation, WIF) in production CI. 27 repos use the org secret BFI_DEVSECOPS_WIF_PROVIDER. For example, bravo-dms-fe deploy-prod.yaml signs in with google-github-actions/auth, id-token: write, and the service account bfi-devsecops-wif@bfi-devsecops.iam.gserviceaccount.com. There is also BFI_BRAVONONPROD_WIF_PROVIDER (June 2026) for non-prod. So option C below reuses a pattern SRE already runs. It is not a new platform.
With SRE: find the service account behind the key and its GCP project. List its roles and its Google Play Console permissions.

Create a new key for the same service account. Update the org secret. Run one build in a backend repo and one build-prod-test (Firebase distribution, not Play) to prove it works. Then disable and delete the old key in GCP.
Raise a follow-up (not Phase 0): a separate service account for Google Play publishing, used only by this repo, and later WIF instead of a key.
In GCP, the service account shows only the new key. The old key is disabled, then deleted.
The org secret shows today's date.
One backend deploy pipeline and one mobile pipeline that uses the key pass after the swap.
A follow-up ticket exists for "separate Play publisher account".

p: Who. SRE (GCP IAM owner) and a GitHub org admin. The mobile squad only verifies the mobile pipeline.

Risks and rollback. Highest-risk step in Phase 0, because it can break deploys of many backend services. Rollback: re-enable the old key in GCP within its deletion grace period, and put the old value back in the org secret. Plan it on a quiet day, with SRE watching, not on a release day.

li.p: Q3: Does SRE agree to rotate an org-wide key for a mobile finding? Who signs it off?
Q6: Which GCP project and service account is it? Does it really hold Google Play permissions plus GCP deploy roles?

td.p: A. SRE rotates the shared key: new key, update the org secret, test, disable the old key, delete it later
The same key still deploys backends and publishes the app. Still a long-lived key in 51 repos

B. Split, with a key: a new service account only for Google Play publishing, its key stored only in customer_app_prod and customer_app_prod_test. Remove Play access from the shared account. SRE also does A
The mobile app no longer depends on an org-wide key. A leak of one key no longer gives both powers

C. Split, with no key: a new Play publisher service account that CI reaches through Workload Identity Federation (google-github-actions/auth, job needs id-token: write). r0adkll/upload-google-play takes serviceAccountJson: ${{ steps.auth.outputs.credentials_file_path }}, which its README documents. Trust limited to repo bfi-finance/bravo-customer-app on release refs. SRE also does A
No key exists, so none can leak. Google's advice is to avoid user-managed keys and use a dedicated service account per application

The existing WIF provider (BFI_DEVSECOPS_WIF_PROVIDER) needs a binding for this repo and a new Play-only service account. The new account must be invited in Play Console. Test on the internal track first

p: Recommended: C for the mobile app, plus A by SRE. The shared key must be rotated anyway, because it was exposed. Moving Google Play to its own keyless account removes the mobile app from the 51-repo blast radius. If the WIF binding takes too long, use B as a stepping stone. Later, outside Phase 0: the Google org policy "Disable service account key creation", with exceptions, as Google recommends.
h2: Where should keys live? (the Cloud KMS question)
p: Short answer: use Cloud KMS for keys that sign something, and use no key at all where Google or GitHub offer keyless sign-in. Cloud KMS keeps a private key inside Google (optionally in an HSM) and does the signing for you. The key never leaves. It is not a place to park a downloaded service-account JSON or an SSH private key for CI to read back. For stored secret values, the matching Google product is Secret Manager, and BFI also runs HashiCorp Vault.

li.p: Cloud KMS in production use: bravo-terraform product/kms defines an HSM-protected key, bfi-go-pkg cryptox and bfi-java-pkg data-encryption use KMS for data encryption, and bravo-customer-bff-service has a KMS data-key sync script.

HashiCorp Vault in project bfi-devsecops, auto-unsealed with the KMS key vault-keyring/vault-key. app-deployment uses it for application runtime secrets. We found no GitHub workflow that reads CI secrets from Vault today.
Keyless Google sign-in for CI (WIF): BFI_DEVSECOPS_WIF_PROVIDER, used by 27 repos, including prod deploys.

td.p: Uploads the app to Google Play (and, in other repos, deploys to GCP)
No key. WIF with a Play-only service account (0.2b option C)
A key in KMS or Secret Manager is still a long-lived key that CI must read. With WIF, CI gets a token that lasts about an hour and only for this repo. Google's advice is to avoid service-account keys
No key. GitHub App token, read-only, 1 hour (0.2a option C)
GitHub cannot check a signature made in KMS during git clone without extra tooling. A short-lived App token removes the key instead of hiding it
Signs the Android bundle before upload
Cloud KMS (HSM) is a good fit, as a later step

Signing is what KMS is for. Cloud KMS has a PKCS#11 library, and Java's jarsigner (used for .aab files) can sign through PKCS#11. CI signs in with WIF, asks KMS to sign, and never holds the private key. If Play App Signing is on (Q14), this key is only the upload key, so a leak can be fixed by asking Google to reset it. Proof of concept needed
Keep in GitHub environment secrets for now, or in an encrypted store such as fastlane match
Apple's codesign reads keys from the macOS keychain. Signing through Cloud KMS is not a common path on macOS runners
Apple offers no keyless sign-in from GitHub. Rotate on a schedule
A personal token from 2022 should not sit in the prod path
Values built into the app (API_SECRET, VIDA_*, DATADOG_CLIENT_TOKEN, …)
Anyone can pull these out of the app, so a vault does not protect them. Plan 01 step 3 (API_SECRET as public) is the real fix

p: Recommended for Phase 0: WIF for Google Play and a GitHub App token for git dependencies. Both remove the key instead of moving it. Cloud KMS for the Android upload key is worth a follow-up ticket (proposed for Phase 2, next to step 2.17 "make R8 explicit"), after a proof of concept. Secret Manager or Vault for CI secrets adds little while the secrets still live in GitHub environments that only release refs can use (0.3).
h2: Step 0.3a: Branch and tag rules on the prod environments (possible today)
p: Why. Today any branch can run a workflow that uses customer_app_prod. That is how "Reveal Secret" could reach prod secrets. A deployment branch and tag policy limits prod secrets to protected refs. This is available on the Team plan.

li.p: All 6 environments have 0 protection rules and no deployment branch policy.
customer_app_prod is used by build-prod.yml (4 jobs) and build-prod-artifact.yml (2 jobs).
customer_app_prod_test is used by build-prod-test.yml (3 jobs). This "test only" workflow also uploads to Google Play with the org key. So it needs the same rule.
Admins can bypass environment rules (can_admins_bypass: true).
Recent tags look like v2.28.0-rc10. There is also a stray tag vnull (probably from a failed tag run).
On customer_app_prod and customer_app_prod_test, set "Deployment branches and tags" to Selected: branches master and release-*, tags v*.
Check how build-prod.yml is started today. It is workflow_dispatch with a tag input. Confirm the release manager runs it from master or a release-* branch, not from a feature branch.
Optional, same ticket: a tag ruleset so only release engineering can create v* tags. Otherwise anyone with write access can create a v* tag and use it to reach prod secrets.
Delete the stray vnull tag (after checking nothing points at it).
GET /repos/.../environments/customer_app_prod shows a deployment_branch_policy. Same for customer_app_prod_test.
A test dispatch of build-prod-test.yml from a feature branch fails at the environment check.
The next real prod release from a release branch still works.

p: Who. Repo admin (Samuel or another admin) and the release manager.

Risks and rollback. If the release process runs from a branch that is not in the list, the prod build is blocked. Rollback: set the policy back to "No restriction" (one click). Agree the branch list with the release manager first.

A real case to settle first (found 20 Oct). On 15 Sep 2026, build-prod.yml was dispatched twice from the branch ci/test-build-prod-android-sdk-2.25.x (one failure, one cancelled). That branch would not match master, release-* or v*. So either (a) such test runs move to build-prod-test.yml on customer_app_prod_test with the same rule, or (b) the rule allows a named pattern such as ci/test-build-prod-*, which weakens it. Recommendation: (a). Ask the release manager who ran those builds and why (Q16).
h2: Step 0.3b: Required reviewers on prod environments (decision)
p: Why. Branch rules (0.3a) stop feature branches. They do not stop someone with admin or bypass rights, or a workflow merged into master or a release branch. Required reviewers would add a human approval before any job sees prod secrets.
Today. Not available. Org plan: Team. Repo: private. GitHub's docs: required reviewers and wait timers are "only available for public repositories" on Free, Pro and Team plans.
Options. See "Options and recommendation (0.3)" below. It covers 0.3a and 0.3b together.

li.p: Q1: Who decides between A, B and C, and by when?
Q8: Can we move CODEOWNERS for .github/ and "require code owner review" into Phase 0? Today CODEOWNERS has one owner for everything (* @samuel-bfi) and the ruleset does not require code-owner review.

td.p: A. Environment branch and tag policy on the 2 prod environments (master, release-*, v*), plus a tag ruleset so only release engineering can create v* tags
Available on our plan. A feature branch can no longer reach prod secrets
Does not stop a bad workflow that is merged into master or a release branch

B. Option A, plus: a push ruleset "Restrict file paths" on .github/workflows/** with a short bypass list (release engineering, SRE). CODEOWNERS for .github/ and "Require review from Code Owners" in the ruleset. Default GITHUB_TOKEN set to read-only, and "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" turned off. Ruleset admin bypass changed from "always" to "pull requests only"
Only named people can change workflows, and the right people review them. A workflow cannot approve its own PR. GitHub's changelog (Sep 2024) says push rules are available on Team for private repos
More settings to own. The bypass list must stay small. The 4 workflows without a permissions: block need one first, so the read-only default does not break them
C. GitHub Enterprise (required reviewers on environments, prevent self-review, no admin bypass), or a separate prod-pipeline repo
Strongest. Enforced by GitHub, not by workflow code
Licence cost for the whole org, or a second repo to maintain. A management decision

p: Recommended: B now, and C recorded as a decision with an owner and a date. B closes most of the gap at no licence cost. Confirm in Settings → Rules that "New push ruleset" is offered before the ticket is sized. If it is not, fall back to A plus CODEOWNERS.

li.p: 314 lines. Header says it builds artifacts only and must not deploy to Firebase, Play or the App Store.
Uses customer_app_prod in 2 jobs, no approval step. Uploads with actions/upload-artifact@v4 (default retention, so the signed files stay downloadable for days).
build-prod-test.yml covers a similar need but also uploads to Play and Firebase.
Ask the squad who uses it and why (Q9).
If nobody needs it: delete it (one PR on master, cherry-pick to release branches if present).
If it is needed: add the same approval-prod job as build-prod.yml (2 approvals) as a needs: dependency of both build jobs. Set retention-days: 1 on the uploads, like build-prod.yml.
Either the file is gone, or a dispatch stops at the approval job and artifacts expire after 1 day.

Risks. None to the app. Someone who relies on it for QA must switch to build-prod-test.yml.

Anyone who uses it moves to build-prod-test.yml
B. Keep it, add the 2-approval job as a needs: dependency, retention-days: 1 on uploads, permissions: contents: read
Keeps the use case, closes the gap
One more prod-signing workflow to maintain
C. Fold it into build-prod.yml as a "distribution: none" choice
One prod workflow, one gate to protect. Matches roadmap step 2.19 (reusable workflows)

Original idea. Once environment reviewers exist, the environment rule replaces the workflow step.

Today the step needs 2 approvals from tribe-bravo-sre, release-engineering, samuel-bfi, subhanbfi. An environment rule needs only 1 of up to 6 reviewers. Removing the step would weaken the gate even with Enterprise, unless we accept 1 approver.

td.p: A. Keep the step as it is
Approvers mix people and teams. The token is the 2022 GH_PAT. The person who starts the run can approve it

B. Harden it: exclude-workflow-initiator-as-approver: true, approvers as teams only, and a GitHub App token instead of GH_PAT. The action's README says team approvers need a GitHub App token with read access to org members and write access to issues
No self-approval. No long-lived personal token in the prod path
App tokens live 1 hour, so the approval window must stay under 60 minutes, or the job fails
C. Replace it with environment required reviewers (needs GitHub Enterprise)

p: Recommended: B. In Phase 0, only the approval step moves to an App token. GH_PAT is used by 7 other workflows here, and maybe by other repos. Replacing it everywhere is a separate ticket (Q11).
h2: Step 0.6: Scan workflow files for printed secrets (Codacy)
p: Why. Stops the next "Reveal Secret" at review time. This is a main control while we stay on the Team plan.

li.p: No such check in this repo. .github/scripts/ has only build-merged-changelog.py.

Codacy is BFI's standard scanner. "Codacy Static Code Analysis" and "Codacy Diff Coverage" are required checks on master and release* here. The shared bfi-base-template pipelines (java-pr-pipeline.yaml, js-pr-pipeline.yaml) default to scanning-tool: codacy and container-scanning-tool: codacy (Codacy CLI v2 container scan).

Other repos keep their Codacy tool list in the repo. 33 repos have a .codacy.yml (mostly exclude_paths, for example bravo-agency-app, also a Flutter app). Several have .codacy/codacy.yaml with a tool list, for example bravo-agent-service: lizard, opengrep, pmd, trivy. This repo has only .codacy/instructions/review.md, so its tool setup lives in the Codacy UI.

Codacy can scan GitHub Actions files. Codacy's supported-tools page lists GitHub Actions with static analysis by Opengrep and secret detection by Opengrep and Trivy. Codacy moved from Semgrep to Opengrep in February 2026.

Pattern on/off switches are UI-only.bravo-backoffice-web-ui.codacy/pattern-cleanup-checklist.md notes that .codacy.yaml supports only paths, engines and languages, so individual patterns are toggled in the Codacy UI by a repo admin.

In Codacy (repo admin): make sure Opengrep and Trivy are on for this repo, including the GitHub Actions patterns. Add .codacy/codacy.yaml with the tool list, like bravo-agent-service, so the setup is visible in the repo.
Test: a test PR with a copy of the old test.yaml. Record which Codacy patterns fire.

Only if Codacy does not flag the "print a secret with spaces" trick: add .github/scripts/check-workflow-secrets.sh. It fails when a run: line both prints (echo, printf, cat, tee, >>) and uses ${{ secrets. Also flag sed/tr/rev/base64 applied to a secret, which is how masking was defeated in test.yaml.
Run that script from a small workflow workflow-lint.yml that triggers on every PR with no paths-ignore (see 0.7). Remove the test.yaml copy after the test.
A PR that adds echo ${{ secrets.X }} fails the check.
A PR that adds echo "${{ secrets.X }}" | sed 's/./& /g' fails the check.
Current workflows on master pass (no false alarm).

p: Who. One mobile engineer, plus a Codacy repo admin for the pattern settings. SRE reviews the pattern list.
Risks. A grep check can be bypassed by a determined insider. It catches mistakes and makes intent visible in review. That is why 0.3b and CODEOWNERS matter too.

td.p: A. Codacy with Opengrep and Trivy on for GitHub Actions files, tool list in .codacy/codacy.yaml. Plus a small grep step only for the pattern Codacy misses, if any

B. Codacy plus a custom Opengrep rule for printing secrets

p: Recommended: A. Codacy is the standard across BFI repos and is already enforced here. Add the grep step only if the test.yaml test shows a gap. Consider B if Codacy supports custom rules. Keep C as an option for later, not Phase 0.
h2: Step 0.7: Run checks on PRs that change only .github/**
p: Why.pr-pipeline.yml has paths-ignore: ".github/**". A PR that only changes workflows runs none of our own checks. That is how a workflow like test.yaml can arrive without any automated check.

li.p: Codacy is a GitHub App, not a workflow, so it already reports on workflow-only PRs. PRs #1493 and #1502 changed only .github/ and merged with the required Codacy checks.
Third-party actions are pinned to commit SHAs since PR #1450 (DM-2600, 7 Oct 2026). Good.
GitHub-owned actions are still on tags (actions/checkout@v4, @v2, setup-java@v3, download-artifact@v2). 42 lines.

update-graphify.yaml (new on 15 Oct) calls a reusable workflow from another repo at @master: bfi-finance/bfi-base-template/.github/workflows/update-graphify.yaml@master. Whatever lands on that branch runs here.

New workflow-lint.yml, triggered on pull_request with no path filter: actionlint, the 0.6 grep step if needed, and a SHA-pin check (allow actions/* on tags for now, or pin them too, decide in Q10). Security scanning stays in Codacy.
Pin the bfi-base-template reusable workflow to a commit SHA, or accept @master and give that repo's .github/ the same protection.
A PR that changes only a workflow file shows the workflow-lint check and cannot merge while it fails (add it to the ruleset's required checks).
actionlint passes on master, or the known findings are listed in the ticket.

p: Who. One mobile engineer. SRE for the ruleset change.
Risks. Making the check required blocks merges if it is flaky. Start as non-required for one week, then make it required.

td.p: A. Rely on Codacy only (it already runs on workflow-only PRs)
No actionlint (YAML and expression errors), no SHA-pin check, no grep step
B. Codacy plus a tiny workflow-lint.yml: no path filter, permissions: contents: read, no secrets. Runs actionlint, the SHA-pin check and the 0.6 grep step if needed. Required after 1 week
Fast and safe. Covers what Codacy does not

C. Option B, plus pin everything to commit SHAs: the 42 GitHub-owned action lines still on tags, and the cross-repo reusable workflow bfi-base-template/...@master. Dependabot for github-actions keeps the pins fresh
GitHub's guidance: pin to a full commit SHA, and treat reusable workflows like third-party actions
Dependabot PRs to review each week. The bfi-base-template pin must be bumped on purpose when the template changes

p: Recommended: C. Codacy does the security scanning. The small job adds the checks Codacy does not do. The pins stop a moved tag, or a change on another repo's master, from running here.

li.p: GitHub, Secure use reference for GitHub Actions: pin to a full commit SHA, CODEOWNERS on .github/workflows, least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC instead of long-lived secrets, never use structured data as a secret, same care for reusable workflows.
GitHub, Deployments and environments: required reviewers only for public repos on Free, Pro and Team; up to 6 reviewers, 1 approval needed; prevent self-review; admin bypass.
GitHub, About rulesets and changelog: push rules generally available (Sep 2024): "Restrict file paths", for example .github/workflows/**/*.
GitHub, actions/create-github-app-token: owner, repositories, permission-* inputs; tokens expire after 1 hour and are revoked at the end of the job.
Google Cloud, Best practices for managing service account keys: avoid user-managed keys, one service account per application, disable before delete, org policy to block key creation.
r0adkll/upload-google-play: serviceAccountJson takes the credentials file from google-github-actions/auth (Workload Identity Federation).
trstringer/manual-approval: exclude-workflow-initiator-as-approver, team approvers need a GitHub App token, 60-minute limit with App tokens.
Codacy, Supported languages and tools: GitHub Actions covered by Opengrep (static analysis) and Opengrep + Trivy (secret detection).
Google Cloud, Cloud KMS PKCS #11 library: lets tools that speak PKCS#11, such as Java's jarsigner, sign with a key held in KMS.
zizmor audits: template-injection, excessive-permissions, unpinned-uses (SHA pins for all actions by default), overprovisioned-secrets, unredacted-secrets, artipacked.
